extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary criticism; creative writers studying Aristotle's Poetics and aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance (expository/commentary) on composing and evaluating epic and tragic poetry and the fine arts according to Aristotelian principles: unity, imitation, character, plausibility, audience, and use of music/spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve lexical ambiguity in context
rubrics_metrics.description: When a word seems to involve some inconsistency of meaning, we should consider how many senses it may bear in the particular passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform close reading: determine whether an apparent inconsistency is due to multiple senses of a term and choose the sense(s) appropriate to the passage rather than presuming error. (Surrounding discussion: critics often jump to groundless conclusions by assuming a single intended meaning.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify impossibilities by artistic requirements or higher reality
rubrics_metrics.description: The impossible must be justified by reference to artistic requirements, or to the higher reality, or to received opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irrational or 'impossible' elements in a work are acceptable if they serve an artistic purpose (idealization, aesthetic effect) or appeal to commonly held belief. Example: Zeuxis' painted men who exceed reality; the ideal may rightly surpass the real.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer probable impossibilities to possible improbabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet working by illusions 'ought to prefer probable impossibilities to possible improbabilities.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing between a highly unlikely-but-coherent fictional element and a technically possible-but-unbelievable one, prefer the version that preserves aesthetic plausibility and coherence of appearance (τὸ πιθανόν). This is central to Aristotle's doctrine of aesthetic semblance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve apparent contradictions with dialectical rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Things that sound contradictory should be examined by the same rules as in dialectical refutation—whether the same thing is meant, in the same relation, and in the same sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the method of testing whether terms or assertions have been used in different senses or relations; seek resolution by reference to what the poet actually says or to what an intelligent reader would tacitly assume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irrational elements or depravity without inner necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of the irrational, and, similarly, depravity of character, are justly censured when there is no inner necessity for introducing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce irrational acts or morally corrupt traits only when they are required by the inner logic of the plot or character motivation; gratuitous aberrations invite justified criticism (examples: Aegeus in Euripides, Menelaus in Orestes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Match form and technique to the audience's refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the more refined art is the higher, and the more refined in every case is that which appeals to the better sort of audience...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the expected audience: epic is addressed to a cultivated audience who need less gesture; tragic performance historically addressed a less refined public. Choose complexity, style, and degree of spectacle appropriate to the audience's capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censure excessive gesture/acting rather than poetic composition
rubrics_metrics.description: This censure attaches not to the poetic but to the histrionic art; gesticulation may be equally overdone in epic recitation or lyric competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on exaggerated physical action or stage business to carry the work; distinguish faults of performers (over-gesticulation, caricatured representation) from the poetic text itself. Action is not condemned per se—only bad, exaggerated performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure textual power independent of physical performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy ... produces its effect even without action; it reveals its power by mere reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for a text that conveys its intended emotional and intellectual effects on the page, not only in enacted spectacle; the work should retain force when read aloud or silently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use music and spectacle as vivid accessories, not substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Music and spectacular effects [are] important accessories; and these produce the most vivid of pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ music, rhythm, visual spectacle to intensify vividness and immediacy, but treat them as enhancements to the artistic whole rather than as replacements for strong plot, character, or language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer concentrated unity; avoid dilution by length
rubrics_metrics.description: The art attains its end within narrower limits; for the concentrated effect is more pleasurable than one which is spread over a long time and so diluted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value compression and focused effect: a shorter, unified imitation often produces more pleasure and impact than a long, diffuse treatment. Consider how length affects intensity and unity of experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate a single action (unity of plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each [poem] is, in the highest degree attainable, an imitation of a single action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose plots with a central, unified action or causal chain; avoid assembling many independent episodes that fragment the unity of the whole. If multiple actions are used, ensure they cohere to a dominant dramatic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce the pleasure proper to the art (fulfil the art's specific end)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each art ought to produce, not any chance pleasure, but the pleasure proper to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the specific kind of aesthetic pleasure the genre should elicit (e.g., tragic catharsis) and shape formal elements—plot, character, language, rhythm—to achieve that specific end rather than merely incidental delights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate human life: character, emotion, and inner action
rubrics_metrics.description: The actual objects of aesthetic imitation are threefold ... ἤθη, πάθη, πράξεις (character, emotions, actions). The πρᾶξις that art seeks to reproduce is mainly an inward process, a psychical energy working outwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus representation on moral character (ἤθη), transient emotions (πάθη), and inwardly-motivated actions (πρᾶξεις); prioritize inner psychological processes and motivations over mere external happenings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use external environment as background to human interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Landscape and animals are not ranked among the objects of aesthetic imitation. The external world only so far as it forms a background of action, and enters as an emotional element into man's life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ setting, scenery, and non-human elements insofar as they illuminate or heighten human motives and feelings, not as ends in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as likeness of sensible appearances, not mere symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: A work of art is a likeness (ὁμοίωμα) or reproduction of an original, and not a symbolic representation of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to reproduce how things appear to the senses (phantasia) rather than rely on purely conventional or arbitrary symbols; art depends on resemblance and sensuous presentation to evoke its effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address the sensibility / imagination (phantasia), not only abstract reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Art addresses itself not to the abstract reason but to the sensibility and image-making faculty; it is concerned with outward appearances; it employs illusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage the reader's imaginative faculty and sensory imagination: use vivid images and plausible illusion ('τὸ πιθανόν') to make the world feel real and to produce aesthetic affect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music should express moral character and help form it
rubrics_metrics.description: Music ... is the express image and reflexion of moral character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If music or rhythm is part of a work (literal or prosodic), use melodic and rhythmic choices to reflect and reinforce character traits and ethical tones; recognise music's formative influence on emotional and moral perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on phantasia for images but recognise its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's psychology does not admit of such a faculty as a creative imagination ... which not merely reproduces objects passively perceived, but fuses together the things of thought and sense, and forms a new world of its own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imagination/phantasia as the image-making faculty that recalls and reshapes sensed impressions for art, but be aware Aristotle's view limits purely free recombination—ground imaginative invention in perceived or intelligible experience to maintain plausibility and verisimilitude.
